title: Big Life Events
description: The same checklist for a move, a marriage, a split, a baby, a lost job, or a death.
wolfLine: The event is loud. The checklist is quiet, and it is the part that saves you.

lessons.title: When the Event Hits
lessons.summary: The event changes. The order of the money work does not.

steps.title: Four beats
steps.body:
A move, a wedding, a divorce, a baby, a lost job, or a death all hit the same list.

Name the bills that changed. Update the [[beneficiary]] names and the insurance. Set the cash plan. Tell the people who share the money.

steps.prompt: Put the money work in order.
items: Tell the people who share the money
steps.explain: You cannot plan a bill you have not listed. The papers and the cash come before the announcement.

steps.prompt: Why do the papers come before you spend the savings?
choices: An old beneficiary can send the money to the wrong person
The bank requires a party first
steps.explain: A wedding, a divorce, or a death is exactly when the old name becomes the wrong name.

steps.prompt: You can skip the list if the event is a happy one.
steps.explain: A wedding and a baby add bills too. Happy is not the same as cheap.

steps.prompt: First, list the bills that ___.
steps.explain: The list is the start. Guessing is how a bill gets missed.

lessons.title: Each Event’s Job
lessons.summary: Match the moment to the money move.

steps.title: Six moments, four cards
steps.body:
Moving cities needs a deposit and a truck. Getting married needs a talk and new beneficiaries. A baby needs childcare and insurance. A lost job needs a cut in bills and the [[emergency fund]].

Divorce and a death get their own lessons. They are not missing. They are next.

steps.prompt: Match the event to the money job.
pairs: Deposits, a truck, and first month’s rent
A money talk and updated beneficiaries
Cut bills and use the emergency fund
steps.explain: Each event has a job. The match is the job, not a slogan.

steps.prompt: You are moving cities. Which pile of cash is the one to plan first?
choices: Deposits, a truck, and the first month
A HELOC on a house you do not own yet
steps.explain: The move has a due date. The other piles do not.

steps.prompt: Losing a job is the moment to raise every subscription.
steps.explain: It is the moment to cut. The emergency fund is for the gap, and it is finite.

steps.prompt: A new baby adds ___ to the monthly plan.
steps.explain: Childcare is the line that shows up and stays.

lessons.title: Update the Papers
lessons.summary: A divorce, a marriage, or a death leaves old names in place until you change them.

steps.title: The transfer does not notice the decree
steps.body:
Accounts and policies keep the old instructions until you change them. This statement still sends **$400** a month to an account only a former spouse can open.

The [[beneficiary]] on a life policy can be just as stale. Update it. Tell the insurer. Do not assume the divorce did the paperwork.

lines.label: Automatic transfer to an account only your former spouse can open

steps.prompt: Which line should have stopped?
steps.explain: The $400 transfer still feeds an account that is no longer yours to share.

lines.label: Automatic transfer to an account only your former spouse can open

steps.prompt: How much is that leftover transfer per year?
You just married. What happens to a life policy that still names a parent, if you wanted your spouse?
choices: Nothing, until you file a beneficiary change
It updates on the wedding day
The court picks a new name
steps.explain: The form is the update. The wedding is not.

steps.prompt: A divorce automatically removes an ex from every beneficiary line.
steps.explain: You have to change each account and each policy. The decree does not log in for you.

lessons.title: A Wedding Budget
lessons.summary: Give the day a total before the vendors do.

steps.title: Eight thousand dollars
steps.body:
The cap is **$8,000**. The venue needs at least **$3,000**. Food needs at least **$2,000**. Photos need at least **$1,000**.

What remains is a buffer. A wedding without a buffer spends the [[emergency fund]] the first time a vendor adds a fee.

steps.prompt: Assign $8,000. The venue needs at least $3,000, food at least $2,000, and photos at least $1,000.
steps.explain: Those three minimums are $6,000. The buffer gets a job too, and all $8,000 is assigned.

steps.prompt: Venue $3,000, food $2,000, and photos $1,000. How much of the $8,000 is still unassigned?
A vendor adds a $400 fee. The buffer is $2,000. How much buffer is left?
If the wedding runs over, the emergency fund is the right next account.
steps.explain: The buffer is for the wedding. The emergency fund is for a job loss or an urgent repair.

lessons.title: A Big Expense
lessons.summary: Divide it by the months you actually have.

steps.title: A move with a date
steps.body:
The move will cost **$6,000**, and you have **10** months. That is **$600** a month.

Waiting and putting it on a card adds [[interest]]. The plan is the $600, set aside on purpose.

steps.prompt: A $6,000 move in 10 months. How much do you set aside each month?
You actually save $600 for 6 months, then the date moves up. How much have you saved?
The move still costs $6,000. How short are you?
What is the better fix for that $2,400 gap?
choices: Cut the move or earn the gap, instead of quietly charging it
Put it on a card and call it a plan
Skip the next month of rent
steps.explain: A card is a loan. Name it as one, or shrink the expense.

lessons.title: Cash or a Loan
lessons.summary: The loan costs $1,000 more for the same day.

steps.prompt: The loan is $750 a month for 12 months. What do you pay in all?
Paying from savings costs $8,000. How much more is the loan?
You have the $8,000, and it is not your emergency fund. Which page costs less?
steps.explain: Savings costs $8,000. The loan costs $9,000.

steps.prompt: The loan is cheaper because you pay it in small pieces.
steps.explain: The pieces add up to $9,000. Small is not the same as less.

steps.prompt: The extra $1,000 on the loan is the cost of ___.
steps.explain: Same wedding. The extra thousand is interest and fees, not a better party.

lessons.title: A Death in the Family
lessons.summary: The papers matter more than the casserole schedule.

steps.title: What to touch first
steps.body:
Ask for the death certificates you will need. Find the will, the [[beneficiary]] forms, and the bills that were on autopay.

A funeral here is budgeted at **$8,000**. If **$3,000** was set aside, the gap is **$5,000**. Do not fill that gap from a credit card before you know what insurance or the estate will pay.

steps.prompt: The funeral budget is $8,000 and $3,000 was set aside. How large is the gap?
Which paper tells the insurer who is paid?
steps.explain: The beneficiary form is the instruction. The other two are not.

steps.prompt: Autopay stops on its own when someone dies.
steps.explain: Bills keep drafting until a person stops them. Find the list.

steps.prompt: The gap in this funeral budget is ___.
steps.explain: $8,000 − $3,000 = $5,000. Know the gap before you borrow it.

lessons.title: Tom’s Year
lessons.summary: The move was affordable. The wedding, on top of it, was not.

story.title: Tom’s year
story.body:
Tom is 32. He moves cities, and the truck, the deposit, and the first month cost **$3,500**. His [[emergency fund]] was **$10,000**, so **$6,500** is left.

The wedding he wants is **$8,000**. Paying it in cash from what remains would leave him **$1,500** short, and it would spend the cushion he has left.

He gets married anyway, on a smaller plan, and he updates his [[beneficiary]]. When a layoff rumor starts in the fall, the remaining savings are still there.

steps.prompt: The emergency fund was $10,000 and the move cost $3,500. How much is left?
The wedding he first wanted is $8,000. How short is the $6,500?
What keeps a cushion for the layoff rumor?
choices: A smaller wedding, so the $6,500 is not spent
The $8,000 wedding, paid from the cushion
Skipping the beneficiary update to save a stamp
steps.explain: The $1,500 gap means the original wedding spends the cushion and still comes up short.

steps.prompt: Tom’s marriage automatically made his spouse the beneficiary.
steps.explain: He had to send the form. The wedding did not.

steps.prompt: If he keeps the $6,500 and a layoff cuts $2,000 of income, how much of the cushion is left after covering that $2,000?

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Big Life Events
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: You divorced last month. A policy still names your ex. What actually changes it?
steps.explain: Each policy keeps its old name until you change that policy.

steps.prompt: A $4,800 expense over 8 months. How much do you set aside each month?
A loan costs $6,600 over the year. Cash costs $6,000. How much more is the loan?
A happy event, like a wedding, has no money checklist.
steps.explain: It has a budget, a beneficiary update, and a line it must not steal from the emergency fund.
